title: Shabazi's Songs of Longing
hookLine: Rabbi Shalom Shabazi, seventeenth-century Yemenite poet, whose songs are still sung
carry: longing for zion, sung inside the joy
tomorrow: a rabbi wanted his people's old ways back. why call it a crown?

cards: The last night of something. The final show, the last shift at a summer job, the last day before everyone scatters.
Somebody starts the song, the one from the beginning, and suddenly everyone is singing and crying at the same time, and nobody wants it to stop. Why does a sad song help?
Because a song can hold two things at once, the joy that it happened and the ache that it's over, without making you choose. The Jews of Yemen had a poet who understood that.

teach.h: HEBREW, ARAMAIC, ARABIC IN ONE SONG.
teach.b: His name was Rabbi Shalom Shabazi.
Tradition remembers him as a poet of Yemen whose songs Yemenite Jews still sing, at weddings, at henna nights before weddings, around the Shabbat table.

He wrote in Hebrew, in Aramaic, and in Arabic, the language of the street around him, sometimes moving between them inside one poem. His songs often carry longing: for Zion, for God's nearness, for a home far away.
And they're sung at the happiest moments of a family's life. That isn't a contradiction. It's what the poems are for.

teach.h: HOW SHALL WE SING IN A FOREIGN LAND?
teach.b: There's an old question in the Psalms, from people far from home: "How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a foreign land?" The Jews of Yemen gave an answer with their whole lives.
You sing it anyway, together, with the longing inside the joy. So here's what this tradition gives you for a week of endings. You don't have to pick between happy and sad.
You don't have to stand alone with either.

teach.h: JOY AND ACHE IN ONE ROOM.
teach.b: You can sing, with other people, a song that holds both, the way a henna night holds a bride's joy and her mother's tears in the same room.
The surprising part: songs remembered under one poet's name are still sung in living rooms and wedding halls today, far from the place they were written.

how: Yemenite Jewish families sing piyyutim attributed to Rabbi Shalom Shabazi at weddings, henna celebrations and Shabbat meals, often with one singer leading and the room answering.

games.q: at a cousin's wedding, the band plays an old song and your aunt, far from the town she grew up in, starts crying. what does Shabazi's tradition suggest?
o: sing along with her; the song is made to hold the joy and the longing together.
ask the band to switch to something upbeat, since a wedding is only for joy.
take her outside until she's calm, since sadness shouldn't be part of the day.
games.why: Shabazi's songs of longing are sung at weddings and henna nights. you don't have to choose between happy and sad, or hold either alone.

practice: If you can, put on one Yemenite Jewish song, a piyyut or a wedding song, and just listen for the sit, eyes open, without looking anything up.
If you can't play music right now, listen to one sound near you instead: a fan, traffic, someone in the next room. Notice whether it holds more than one feeling at once.
